rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The people have accumulated the filth that kindles God's anger, so His punishment is now imminent.
rows.anchor: they have gathered all the filth that can ignite God’s anger. His torment is now at hand.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hud's question answers the people's appeal to ancestral worship: they quarrel over deities whose names have no divine sanction or proven existence.
rows.anchor: are you quarrelling with me about those imaginary names which you and your forefathers have kept, about which God has revealed no sanction?

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The people acknowledge that God's existence is indisputable and evidenced, but Islahi asks what proof exists for their idols.
rows.anchor: they know that His existence is indisputable and they have its proof; but as for these idols, what proof of existence do they have?

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Punishment is certain because the people deserve it, although its arrival remains God's prerogative; both sides must wait.
rows.anchor: The advent of punishment is a certainty as they have made themselves worthy of it. However, it is God’s prerogative of bringing it forth.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Once truth has been conclusively conveyed, God's established practice is to rescue the messenger and companions by special grace and destroy the rest.
rows.anchor: the established practice of God that necessarily manifests itself once the truth has been conclusively conveyed. Through His special grace and favour

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A nation is destroyed when stubbornness shows it has no remaining capacity to accept faith; the verse's phrase about not believing signals this.
rows.anchor: This decisive punishment comes when a nation because of its stubbornness and obduracy shows that it has no capacity left in it to accept faith.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Thamūd were remnants of the ‘Ād, also called the second ‘Ād, and lived in northwestern Arabia; some may have survived destruction and migrated north to Ḥijr.
rows.anchor: The Thamūd are from among the remnants of the ‘ Ād and are also called the second ‘Ād. They lived in north west Arabia.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an and Arab tradition describe the ‘Ād and Thamūd similarly, and some poets write as though there were no distinction between them.
rows.anchor: The attributes of the ‘ Ād and the Thamūd are very similarly mentioned in the Qur’ ān and Arab traditions. Some poets mention them in a way as if there is no difference between them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qayl and Qaydār, leaders of the two peoples associated with their punishment, became proverbial in Arabic literature and seem to have shared traits.
rows.anchor: The leaders of both – Qayl and Qaydā r – because of which these nations were punished, have become proverbial in Arabic literature

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṣāliḥ answered the demand for a punishment sign by warning that the people's luxurious life and prosperity would end; they should fear God, heed him, and avoid disorderly leaders.
rows.anchor: They form Ṣāliḥ’s answer to his nation’s demand for punishment. He repeatedly warned them that they must not think that their days of comfort will remain forever.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṣāliḥ designated the she-camel as God's sign and protection: harming her would bring punishment, leaving the people with no shield against it.
rows.anchor: If they harm her, they would be inflicted with God’s punishment. She is a shield for them against God’s punishment. If they break it, then nothing will be able to save them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Attributing the camel to God meant dedicating her as sacrificial animals are dedicated in Islam; harming such a dedicated animal is a grave crime.
rows.anchor: Ascribing the she-camel to God meant that it was dedicated to God the way animals of sacrifice are dedicated to Him in Islam.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The camel tested the people: killing her would prove their oppressors would dare kill Ṣāliḥ as a liar, the point at which the messenger must migrate and punishment falls.
rows.anchor: This she-camel was earmarked by Ṣāliḥ (sws) as a feeler: if they kill her, it would be a certain proof that now these oppressors will show the audacity to kill Ṣāliḥ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an does not indicate that the she-camel had extraordinary physical features; its sign was the consequence of harming her.
rows.anchor: From no word of the Qur’ ān is it indicated that this she-camel was a sign because of having some extra-ordinary features in her form.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi knows of no authentic narration that the she-camel emerged from a mountain or hillock, and says such a report merits no importance.
rows.anchor: To the best of my knowledge, there is no authentic narrative that says that this she-camel was born from a mountain or a hillock. For this reason, it should not be given any importance.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Arabic word āyah means a sign or indication.
rows.anchor: The word آﻳﺔmeans “sign” and “indication.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The camel was marked as a punishment sign in answer to the demand for one; Qur’anic accounts say punishment came on the third day after the leader hamstrung her, with details in several sūrahs.
rows.anchor: This she-camel was demarcated as a sign of punishment in response to the demand that such a sign be presented. Thus it is mentioned in the Qur’ān that when the leader of the Tham ūd hamstrung her, the punishment descended on them on the third day.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Giving a sign instead of immediate punishment demonstrates God's mercy: He delays wrath, hastens mercy, and grants time for those willing to heed the warning.
rows.anchor: instead of sending punishment at the demand of the Tham ūd, a sign for punishment was given. This signifies God’s mercy. He shows delay in wrath and haste in mercy.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the people killed the camel, the Qur’an indicates they received a further three days to abandon their evil ways.
rows.anchor: from other instances of the Qur’ ān that they were given a further respite of three days so that even then if they wanted they could desist from their evil ways.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The camel could graze wherever she wished, was to be left alone, and had a separate drinking day; this tested the people by exposing their malice and animosity.
rows.anchor: This directive was meant to test the nation so that the malice and animosity they have is exposed and nothing remains concealed.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Thamūd held power in Ḥijr and left architectural remains; Quraysh knew their account and settlements from their travels to Syria.
rows.anchor: While travelling to Syria, the Quraysh used to pass by their settlements. For this reason, they were fully aware of their account and had also observed the place they lived.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṣāliḥ recalled their succession to the ‘Ād to remind a power-drunk people of God's greater power: He would deal with them as with the ‘Ād, by the same standard.
rows.anchor: If Ṣāliḥ (sws) reminded them of their position of authority as successors of the ‘Ād nation, it was, as mentioned earlier, to not forget the power of God while being themselves inebriated with power.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jabal and sahl are opposites: the first denotes hilly country, while the second is flat land at the foot of hills.
rows.anchor: The words ﺟﺒﻞand ﺳﻬﻞare opposites. The former means a hilly area and the latter refers to flat land at the based of hills.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Thamūd built grand palaces both by carving hilly terrain and on flat land; surviving structures display their construction skill.
rows.anchor: They constructed grand palaces both in hilly areas by carving them out and also in flat areas of land. Some of their feats of construction still exist.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṣāliḥ lamented their building passion at its height: grand construction signals decadence rather than progress, and towering buildings become tombs inhabited by wild animals; they should remember God and avoid disorder.
rows.anchor: This shows that constructing grand buildings is not a sign of development of a nation; it is in fact a sign of its decadence. These sky scrapers ultimately become its tombs and graveyards

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Messengers are first accepted by the poor and weak because they lack the arrogance that most obstructs acceptance of truth; Islahi relates this to his discussion of Satan and Adam.
rows.anchor: The invitation of a messenger is first always accepted by the poor and the weak because they are devoid of arrogance and it is this arrogance which is the greatest hindrance in accepting the truth.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The arrogant elders' question about Ṣāliḥ's mission is sarcastic, implying that believers are naïve to think he is God's messenger.
rows.anchor: The question “do you think that Ṣāliḥ has been sent by his Lord?” posed by the arrogant individuals of Tham ūd to the believers was sarcastic in nature.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The believers go beyond acknowledging Ṣāliḥ's prophethood and affirm strong conviction in the truth of his message.
rows.anchor: They did not merely confine themselves to acknowledging the messengerhood of Ṣāliḥ (sws), they expressed their strong conviction at the veracity of his real message.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The believers' forceful answer showed that those formerly subservient would no longer submit when truth was at stake.
rows.anchor: Such was the nature of this stern and assertive answer that it proved that those who were hitherto subservient will not any longer remain subservient in the matter of the truth.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage begins to explain that poor and weak people first profess faith in God's messengers.
rows.anchor: though initially the poor and the weak first

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Poor and weak believers are persuaded by the messenger's arguments, not miracles; the arrogant keep demanding signs until punishment finally opens their eyes.
rows.anchor: what appeals to them is the strength in arguments presented by the messenger and not by any miracles. On the other hand, those who claim to be superior and intelligent remain entangled in the demand of miracles and signs

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The arrogant people's declaration of disbelief expresses their final dismay.
rows.anchor: These words express the final dismay of the arrogant elements.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb ʿaqara means to hamstring either a male or a female camel.
rows.anchor: means to hamstring a male or a female camel.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When ʿatā is used with ʿan, it combines the senses of arrogance and disobedience.
rows.anchor: it encompasses the meanings of both arrogance and disobedience.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Killing the camel was the nation's ultimate rebellion and a challenge to Ṣāliḥ to bring the punishment he had threatened.
rows.anchor: This was the ultimate step of rebelliousness taken by the nation. By killing the she-camel, they challenged Ṣāliḥ (sws) to bring the punishment he was threatening them with.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This was Ṣāliḥ's final rejection; further delay would have led to his murder, so punishment came on the third day.
rows.anchor: This was the final expression of his nation in denying Ṣālih (sws). Any further respite given to them would have resulted in their killing him. Because of this reason, the punishment visited them on the third day.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although only the rebellious leader hamstrung the camel, Sūrah al-Shams specifies the individual; the whole nation is charged with the act because all consented.
rows.anchor: as is specified in S ūrah Shams; however, since everyone consented to this heinous act, her killing is ascribed to the whole nation.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rajfah means a shudder or jolt and denotes the punishment that struck the Thamūd.
rows.anchor: It signifies the punishment that visited the nation of Thamūd.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an depicts this punishment elsewhere as a ṣayḥah (54:31), ṣāʿiqah (41:13), and al-ṭāghiyah (69:5).
rows.anchor: At another instance (54:31), the word

rows.speaker: Ḥamīd al-Dīn Farāhī
rows.claim: Farāhī's synthesis describes the ‘Ād and Thamūd's destruction as involving winter clouds, storm winds, horrific thunder, and a deafening shout, with wind as the destructive cause.
rows.anchor: Ustādh Ḥamīd al-Dīn Farāhī in his exegesis of S ūrah al-Dhāriyāt has discussed in detail the nature of punishments
